learn.hook: A plan to run a hospital is just paper until someone decides who does surgery, who runs the pharmacy and who reports to whom. That is organising.
points: Organising is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be performed, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so that people can work together to achieve objectives.
Step 1 Identification and division of work: the total work is divided into manageable activities as per plans, avoiding duplication.
Step 2 Departmentalisation: similar activities are grouped into departments, units or sections, e.g. by function (production, finance) or by product or territory.
Step 3 Assignment of duties: jobs are allocated to members of each department according to their skills (the right person for the right job).
Step 4 Establishing reporting relationships: each person knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report, creating a hierarchy.

example.q: A new school's principal lists all tasks, forms academic, sports and admin wings, gives each teacher duties, and decides that wing heads report to her. Name the steps in order.
steps: Listing all tasks = identification and division of work
Forming wings = departmentalisation
Giving teachers duties = assignment of duties
Wing heads report to principal = establishing reporting relationships
example.answer: Division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, reporting relationships

topics.title: Organisation structure, span of management and functional structure

learn.hook: If one manager can handle 8 people well, how many managers does a team of 64 need? The answer shapes the whole organisation chart.
points: Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. It specifies relationships between people, work and resources.

Span of management is the number of subordinates that can be effectively managed by a superior. It determines the levels of management: a narrow span gives more levels (a tall structure) and a wide span gives fewer levels (a flat structure).
Functional structure groups jobs of a similar nature by function, e.g. production, purchase, marketing, finance, HR, each under a head reporting to the top.
Suitable when the organisation is large, has diversified activities and operations need a high degree of specialisation.

Advantages: occupational specialisation, better control and coordination within a department, managerial efficiency, minimal duplication (economies of scale), easier training, attention to all functional areas. Disadvantages: less emphasis on overall objectives (functional empires), coordination problems across departments, conflicts of interest, and inflexibility (narrow perspective).

example.q: A firm has 48 workers. If each supervisor can handle 6 workers and each manager can handle 4 supervisors, how many supervisors and managers are needed?
steps: Supervisors = 48 ÷ 6 = 8
Managers = 8 ÷ 4 = 2
So 8 supervisors and 2 managers (a wider span would need fewer of both)

topics.title: Divisional structure and comparison with functional

learn.hook: A company that makes cosmetics, edible oils and steel tubes can't run them all from one marketing department. Enter the divisional structure.
points: Divisional structure groups activities by product lines (or regions); each division is a separate unit with its own functions (production, marketing, finance) and a divisional manager responsible for profit or loss.
Suitable for firms that make a large variety of products using different productive resources, or for firms that are growing and diversifying.

Advantages: product specialisation develops varied skills in divisional heads and prepares them for higher posts; each division's profit or loss can be measured, which fixes accountability; quick decisions due to autonomy; easy expansion by adding new divisions.

Disadvantages: conflict among divisional heads over funds and resources; higher costs due to duplication of activities across divisions; divisional managers may put their own division's interest above the organisation's.

Comparison: functional is based on functions, divisional on products; functional gives functional specialisation, divisional gives product specialisation; responsibility is hard to fix in functional, easy in divisional; functional has low cost (no duplication), divisional has high cost (duplication); divisional heads get wider training for top jobs; coordination across functions is harder in functional and easier within a divisional unit.

example.q: Prakriti Ltd makes soaps, juices and cricket bats. Should it use functional or divisional structure? Give one advantage.
steps: The products are very different and need different resources.
So each product should have its own unit with its own functions.
Advantage: the profit of each product division can be measured and its head held responsible.
example.answer: Divisional structure; it allows clear accountability for each product's performance

learn.hook: The org chart says who reports to whom. The lunch table says who actually talks to whom. Both shape how work gets done.
points: Formal organisation: the structure deliberately designed by management, with clearly defined authority, responsibility and relationships. Features: specifies relationships, is a means to achieve objectives, coordinates efforts, is designed by top management, places emphasis on work and rules.

Advantages of formal: easy to fix responsibility, no overlapping, unity of command, easier achievement of goals and stability. Disadvantages: delays due to the scalar chain, ignores social needs (human relationships), and may not recognise creativity and talent.

Informal organisation: a network of social relationships that emerges spontaneously from interaction among employees. Features: originates within the formal organisation, behaviour is shaped by group norms, communication has no fixed direction (grapevine), has no definite structure.

Advantages of informal: faster spread of information and quick feedback, fulfils social needs and sense of belonging, compensates for gaps in the formal structure. Disadvantages: spreads rumours, may resist change, pressure to conform to group norms.

Comparison: formal arises from rules and is deliberately created; informal arises from social interaction and emerges on its own. Formal authority comes from position; informal from personal qualities. Formal follows the scalar chain and is rigid; informal has no fixed path and is flexible. Formal leaders are managers; informal leaders are chosen by the group.

steps: The group formed on its own through a shared interest.

This is informal organisation; a risk is that rumours or distorted news may spread.
example.answer: Informal organisation; it may spread rumours

learn.reallife: In many Indian offices, a common 'chai break' group becomes an informal organisation where news, tips and support travel faster than official emails.

learn.hook: A manager who tries to do everything herself burns out. A manager who hands over work but stays answerable for results grows a team. That is delegation.
points: Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. The manager remains accountable for the final outcome.
Authority: the right of an individual to command subordinates and act within the scope of the position. It arises from formal position and flows downward. It can be delegated.
Responsibility: the obligation of a subordinate to properly perform the assigned duty. It arises from the superior-subordinate relationship and flows upward. It cannot be entirely delegated.
Accountability: answerability for the final outcome. It arises from responsibility, flows upward and cannot be delegated at all. Authority should match responsibility.
Importance: effective management (managers focus on important work), employee development, motivation of employees, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, and better coordination.

revise.summary: Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate, while the superior stays accountable. Authority flows down, responsibility and accountability flow up.
focus: Know which can be delegated and the direction each flows
remember: Authority can be delegated; responsibility cannot be entirely delegated; accountability cannot be delegated at all
Authority flows downward; responsibility and accountability flow upward
traps: Don't confuse delegation with decentralisation
Accountability does not move down with authority
Responsibility (duty to perform) is not accountability (answerability for outcome)

learn.hook: A pizza chain lets each outlet manager decide local offers and staffing on the spot. Head office keeps only big decisions. That is decentralisation.
points: Decentralisation means delegating decision-making authority systematically to the lowest levels, except that which can be exercised only at central points.
Centralisation keeps decision making with a few at the top. No organisation is fully centralised or fully decentralised: a balance is needed, and it shifts as the firm grows.

Importance: develops initiative among subordinates; develops managerial talent for the future; quick decision making; relief to top management; facilitates growth; better control (performance of each level can be evaluated).

Delegation vs decentralisation: delegation is a compulsory act (no manager can do everything) while decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management. Delegation keeps more control with the superior; decentralisation gives more freedom. Delegation's scope is narrow (superior and immediate subordinate); decentralisation's scope is wide (extends to the lowest level).
Purpose: delegation reduces the burden on the manager; decentralisation increases the role of subordinates by giving them more autonomy.

example.q: Swift Couriers lets each branch head decide hiring, local pricing and vendor contracts, while the board decides only on new cities. Is this delegation or decentralisation? Give one benefit.
steps: Authority is spread systematically to the lowest levels across the whole firm.
It is a policy decision by top management.
So it is decentralisation; one benefit is quick decision making at branches.
example.answer: Decentralisation; quicker decisions at the branch level

revise.summary: Decentralisation is delegating decision-making authority systematically to the lowest levels, except what must stay at central points. A balance with centralisation is needed.
